items.description: Ottawa is adding new express entry points for permanent residency applicants in “high-wage” jobs.

items._ogDesc: Ottawa is adding new express entry points for permanent residency applicants in “high-wage” jobs.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Ottawa is adding new express entry points for permanent residency applicants in “high-wage” jobs.

The government also plans to remove the requirement for an employer to prove they can’t find a qualified Canadian for those jobs.

Immigration Minister Lena Diab’s two-pronged announcement in Kitchener, Ont., first adds new express entry points for people with Canadian work experience or with a job offer in a high-wage field such as engineering.

The government considers a high-wage job as one with pay that is at least 1.3 times the median wage, with more express entry points given the higher the wage is.

The government is also introducing a temporary policy to remove the need for an employer to include a Labour Market Impact Assessment on a qualifying job that’s eligible for the new express entry points.

These new policies are set to take effect on Nov. 3.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Tesla says it is pausing orders for its Chinese-made sedan Model 3 Premium in Canada, citing a high demand for the vehicle that used up its import quota from China. Statistics show that the overall quota for 49,000 imported Chinese electrical vehicles has not been used up.
items.body:
Tesla says it is pausing orders for its Chinese-made sedan Model 3 Premium in Canada, citing a high demand for the vehicle that used up its import quota from China. Statistics from the federal government show that the overall quota for 49,000 imported Chinese electrical vehicles during the 12 months beginning March 1 has not been used up.

The claim

A banner appearing on top of Tesla’s website for its Model 3 claims that orders for Premium are paused after “high demand exhausted Tesla’s import quota,” alluding to the government of Canada’s partnership with China to import 49,000 electric vehicles a year at a lower tariff of 6.1 per cent from the previous 100 per cent.

The banner added: “Ordering resumes if Govt of Canada issues more quota, expected March 2027.”

Its Model 3 Performance vehicles, which are more expensive than Premium, are still available to Canadians.

The facts

The federal government in January reached a deal with Beijing to slash tariffs on 49,000 Chinese EVs in exchange for China dropping duties on canola seeds.

That brought tariffs back down to single digits from 100 per cent duties on Chinese EVs imposed in late 2024. Back then, former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s government had argued cheap, heavily subsidized EVs being sold in the North American market constituted a threat to the auto sector.

The quota for 49,000 EVs is split up in two six-month periods: March 1 to Aug. 31, 2026, and Sept. 1, 2026 to Feb. 28, 2027. The first period allotted 24,500 units, while the current period would allow 24,500 units plus any unused units from the previous period, according to the federal Department of Global Affairs.

During the first six months, Global Affairs Canada says 15,603 electric vehicles were imported from China. That means 8,897 units will roll over in the current period, increasing the quota for the second half to 33,397 units.

The quota was implemented on a first-come, first-served basis for an initial period of six months. It is not clear whether the second half of the program is still running on a first-come, first-served basis, and Global Affairs did not immediately respond to questions about the timeline.

For the month of September, only 328 Chinese EVs were imported, according to Global Affairs.

Global Affairs spokesperson Rachael Dolan said in an email the agency does not disclose the names of companies or details of any shipments, “including anticipated quota use, due to commercial confidentiality considerations.”

But Prime Minister Mark Carney has said most Chinese EVs entering Canada are Teslas. “Historically, they’re all Teslas. It looks like most of the ones that’ll come in are Teslas as well in the short term,” he said at the Economic Club of New York on May 28.

Daniel Ross, director of strategic market insights at auto data tracking company Canadian Black Book, estimated 97 per cent of all Chinese vehicles that were imported this year were Teslas.

The company’s data showed 259 Lincoln Nautilus Hybrids, 18 Lotus Eletres and an estimated 200 Polestar 2s were shipped between March and September 2026. The remainder were estimated to be Teslas, he said. It’s unclear how many of those were Tesla Model 3 Premiums.

Tesla did not respond to questions about the pause.

Tesla already had a strong presence for its Chinese EVs, even before Ottawa allowed them in Canada — and before the federal government imposed the 100 per cent tariff.

A 2024 RBC report shows total EV imports from Shanghai amounted to $2.3 billion, or 13.3 per cent of total imports in 2023, a massive increase from $116 million in 2022.

The automaker manufactures Model 3 and Model Y vehicles at its Gigafactory Shanghai plant that opened in 2019 — its first factory abroad, according to Tesla’s website. The Shanghai plant has a capacity to produce about 950,000 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles a year, while its California plant produces about 550,000 vehicles, according to Tesla’s second-quarter 2026 update.

In Canada, the starting price for the Chinese-made Model 3 Premium is close to $40,000, and many vehicles started arriving in full flow this summer, according to DesRosiers Automotive Consultants Inc.’s September auto sales report.

Prices are significantly lower compared to the $73,000 starting price for the Model 3 Performance, according to Tesla’s website.

In the second year of the EV tariff deal, 10 per cent of the quota will be reserved for vehicles under $35,000. Tesla does not have EVs under $35,000 at the moment.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

Ritika Dubey, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Stocks on Wall Street are mixed Friday as another pullback in big technology companies weighs on the market.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Stocks on Wall Street are mixed Friday as another pullback in big technology companies weighs on the market.

The S&P 500 was down 0.1 per cent and on track for a weekly loss. The benchmark index remains near the all-time high it set last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 226 points, or 0.4 per cent, as of 11 a.m. Eastern time.

The Nasdaq composite was down 0.7 per cent and headed for its first weekly loss in five weeks. Weakness for AI stocks has been a major drag on the tech-heavy index this week.

Despite the uneven start, the majority of U.S. stocks were rising.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

Technology companies were the biggest drag on the broader market. Micron Technology fell 3.3 per cent, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 3.1 per cent, Broadcom was down 1.8 per cent and Intel lost 2.9 per cent.

It’s been a choppy week for chipmakers and other big tech stocks central to the artificial intelligence industry. Investors are now worried that the companies, which have relied on debt markets to finance an investment spree into their technology, may not be able to keep borrowing and spending as heavily with yields in bond markets worldwide recently climbing to their highest levels in years.

Netflix’s stock fell 1.9 per cent a day after the company announced that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice. The news comes just days after Netflix said that it plans to lay off about 6 per cent of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions.

Gains by big banks and other financial companies helped limit the market slide. JPMorgan rose 2.3 per cent, Citigroup gained 2.7 per cent and Wells Fargo was up 1.8 per cent.

European markets were broadly higher and Asian markets rose.

In the bond market, Treasury yields mostly eased. The yield on the 10-year Treasury held steady at 5.10 per cent. It had topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002 because of worries about high inflation, signals of a strong U.S. economy and other factors.

Yields are down despite reports this week showing that inflation at the consumer and wholesale level rose more in the U.S. than economists expected.

  • Latest updates on investing here

The reports could persuade the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve to hike their key interest rate before the end of this year. The central bank increased its key interest rate by a quarter-point to about 3.9 per cent in September, its first increase in three years.

Wall Street traders expect the Fed will keep its short-term rate unchanged at policy meeting this month, but the odds of a rate increase at the December meeting have jumped to 76.1 per cent from 50.2 per cent a month ago, according to data from the CME Group.

On Friday, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh offered no fresh signals about potential interest rate policy moves by the Fed while attending a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok.

Elsewhere in the market, shares in Tesla rose 0.6 per cent after the electric vehicle company unveiled a new model of its Roadster sports car that can thrust itself up in the air.

Alcoa jumped 8.8 per cent after reporting quarterly results that topped Wall Street estimates.

Expectations are high for growth in profits from all kinds of companies this reporting season, which began in earnest this week. That’s what’s allowed U.S. stocks to set records despite high inflation and the many other worries weighing on Wall Street.

In energy markets, oil prices remained elevated as the global oil supply continues to be under pressure without a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the Iran war.

  • Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

Brent crude, the international standard, was up 0.1 per cent at US$105.85 per barrel. That is still high compared with around US$72 a barrel in late February before the start of the war. Brent climbed into triple digits last month, the first time since July.

The national average for gasoline is at US$4.33 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA. While that’s lower than the US$4.37 a gallon that it averaged last month, it’s sharply higher than the US$3.06 a gallon from a year ago.

Oil remains well-supported as uncertainties surrounding the situation in the Middle East and concerns over oil flows in the Strait of Hormuz had the market “pricing in a significant risk premium,” ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a commentary Friday.

Alex Veiga, The Associated Press

items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada will get a raft of fresh data to start next week as it weighs what could be a pivotal interest rate decision at the end of the month.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada will get a raft of fresh data to start next week as it weighs what could be a pivotal interest rate decision at the end of the month.

Statistics Canada is set to release its September inflation data on Monday, giving the central bank a look at how energy price pressures are influencing other parts of the consumer basket.

A Reuters poll of economists expects the annual rate of inflation rose to 3.2 per cent in September, up from three per cent in August, according to LSEG Data & Analytics.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

RBC assistant chief economist Nathan Janzen said he expects inflation held steady at three per cent last month. Persistently high gasoline prices tied to the ongoing war in Iran will remain the biggest fuel for inflation, he said.

“We know that energy prices are high. What we don’t know yet is the extent that those higher energy prices have or are going to spill over to broader inflation pressures,” Janzen said.

The Bank of Canada signalled at the start of the Middle East conflict last spring that it would look through a temporary rise in energy costs tied to the war. But officials have warned that the longer global oil prices remain high, the greater the risks that inflation spreads past the gas pump.

In that case, the central bank could be forced to raise its policy rate, which has stood for nearly a year at 2.25 per cent. Most economists consider that level to be modestly stimulative to growth.

Janzen said the Bank of Canada’s upcoming decision on Oct. 28 will be a “live” meeting, where the door is open for the central bank to raise its policy rate, but a hike is not his base case scenario.

Even if the September price data shows signs inflationary pressures are spreading past the gas pumps, Janzen said the central bank will be weighing that against signs of softness in the labour market and wider economy.

Statistics Canada reported last week that the economy shed 68,000 jobs in September, a second consecutive month of falling employment. A re-escalating trade dispute with the United States has also hampered growth prospects heading into the fourth quarter.

  • Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca

“Higher energy prices — all else equal — would mean broader inflation pressures would be expected to rise in the future. But if the economy is getting weaker, then there are some offsetting disinflationary forces there as well,” Janzen said.

“It puts (the Bank of Canada) still in a wait-and-see mode — very, very data dependent.”

The Bank of Canada will also release its own quarterly surveys of businesses and consumers on Monday, which can give the bank a better sense of whether firms are planning to pass their own rising costs on to consumers.

Janzen said inflation expectations and business confidence will help inform the central bank whether higher prices among producers could be passed on to store shelves in the months to come.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items.title: Tesla’s new Roadster car can thrust itself in the air. But don’t expect to drive it anytime soon
items.description: Tesla has unveiled its new Roadster sports car, which can thrust itself up in the air. But drivers shouldn’t expect to take it for a spin anytime soon.
items._ogDesc: Tesla has unveiled its new Roadster sports car, which can thrust itself up in the air. But drivers shouldn’t expect to take it for a spin anytime soon.
items.body:
CHICAGO — Tesla has unveiled its new Roadster sports car, which can thrust itself up in the air. But drivers shouldn’t expect to take it for a spin anytime soon.

Elon Musk’s car company this week debuted the latest bells and whistles of its second generation Roadster — chief among them, as shown off at a Thursday event, are a set of cold gas thrusters and a “multi-mode” suction system that can fling the car in the air for short spurts and spin the vehicle mid-flight.

“Turns out the future does have flying cars,” Musk, Tesla’s CEO, wrote on his social media platform X shortly after.

Thursday’s launch arrived after years of delays and anticipation around the new Roadster — and Tesla shares climbed about 2 per cent in morning trading on Friday after its unveiling.

Still, Musk said production for consumers won’t begin until 2028. Tesla also didn’t immediately set a price tag on its latest electric vehicle.

And of course, these kinds of cars aren’t flinging themselves in the air on highways and streets just yet. There are ample regulatory hurdles for flying vehicles overall. The fine print of the Roadster’s “rocket” feature on Tesla’s website notes: “Not approved for public road use.”

items._ogDesc: A company pursuing an ambitious wind and hydrogen development in Nova Scotia says it now has plans for a $10-billion AI data centre in Cape Breton.
items.body:
POINT TUPPER — A company pursuing an ambitious wind and hydrogen development in Nova Scotia says it now has plans for a $10-billion AI data centre in Cape Breton.

EverWind Fuels says an unnamed “leading frontier AI developer” has signed a 20-year lease.

A statement from the company describes the proposed project in Point Tupper, N.S., as the largest private investment in Nova Scotia’s history.

EverWind says the plan includes $8 billion to build a data centre campus and $2 billion to advance onshore wind energy projects, creating 2,000 construction jobs and 215 permanent positions.

Data centres are typically massive operations that require immense amounts of electricity to run and cool off computer servers.

EverWind says it will protect the province’s electricity users from price hikes while safeguarding water resources, which are typically used as sources of coolant.

EverWind CEO Trent Vichie issued a statement saying Nova Scotians have helped build major projects across Canada, often leaving home to find well-paying work.

“With this investment, we’re creating more opportunities for people to find jobs and build their careers at home in rural Nova Scotia,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Carpenters build new homes in Ottawa on Monday, June 1, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Sean Kilpatrick]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Sean Kilpatrick</media:credit>

OTTAWA — Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. says the annual pace of housing starts in September rose three per cent compared with August.

The national housing agency says the seasonally adjusted annual rate of housing starts for September came in at 248,896 units, up from 242,223 in August.

The result came as actual monthly housing starts in communities with a population of 10,000 or more fell 11 per cent compared with a year ago to 19,984 units in September compared with 22,375 in September 2025.

  • Most recent real estate news from BNNBloomberg.ca

The annual pace of rural starts was estimated at 18,094 units.

The six-month moving average of the seasonally adjusted annual rate was up 0.6 per cent at 250,411 units.

Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist at CMHC, says Canada still faces a long-term housing supply gap and unless housing construction levels increase, improvements in housing affordability since 2023 will be difficult to sustain.

items.body:
For the second day in a row, the federal government is announcing plans to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to train more skilled workers in Canada.

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu is in her home riding of Thunder Bay today rolling out a plan to spend up to $258.6 million over the next five years to train workers in critical sectors, with annual funding of $50 million in the years to follow.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the creation of a Sectoral Workforce Innovation Fund a little over a year ago and the government opened applications for the program in August.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The fund aims to fill the gaps between workers’ skills and industry requirements in sectors like energy or critical minerals by funding projects that could speed up training or certification.

Hajdu’s announcement comes a day after Ottawa unveiled $430 million in spending to help unions and other organizations cover costs for new training facilities and equipment.

The Liberals have announced billions of dollars in spending to train up to 100,000 new skilled workers over the next half decade to support the government’s ambitious infrastructure agenda.

items.title: Former Ontario mortgage broker settles unlicensed fronting case
items.description: Regulator trims penalty as broker admits relying on an unlicensed referrer to vet borrowers
items.content: <p>Regulator trims penalty as broker admits relying on an unlicensed referrer to vet borrowers</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639277602168654143.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Regulator trims penalty as broker admits relying on an unlicensed referrer to vet borrowers
items.body:
A former Ontario mortgage broker who let an unlicensed referral agent handle her client intake has agreed to pay $40,000 to the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA), settling a case in which the regulator had sought more than twice that amount.

Paramjeet Kaur, whose broker licence through Trillium Mortgage Services Inc. expired on March 31, admitted to six breaches of the Mortgage Brokerages, Lenders and Administrators Act, 2006 and its regulations, including facilitating illegal conduct and giving lenders false or deceptive information.

The order, dated Sept. 24, replaces the $85,000 in penalties FSRA proposed in April. The final figure is about 47% of that amount.

How the unlicensed referral pipeline worked

The case began with a May 1, 2024, complaint from a borrower, identified as MA, who said the mortgage registered on her Hamilton property was higher than the amount she had agreed to. She told investigators she had never met Kaur and did not know Trillium was her brokerage.

According to the agreed facts, Vatsal Pareshkumar Khamar, also known as Vic Kumar, answered a Kijiji ad Kaur placed in 2023 and began referring clients to her.

Khamar, who has never held a licence, met eight groups of borrowers, collected their identification and financial documents and obtained signatures.

Kaur prepared the applications and sent them to lenders through Trillium. She relied on Khamar to confirm the borrowers’ identities and never met any of them in person.

Kaur admitted listing one borrower as single when she was married, supplying inaccurate employment and income details for that borrower and overstating MA’s income.

FSRA’s April notice said she knew MA was a low-income college student and earned approximately $90,000 in commissions on the files. Trillium collected roughly $11,000.

“Kaur knew that Khamar was unlicensed, and yet relied on him to complete some of the fundamental obligations of a Mortgage Broker and facilitated his conduct,” the notice said.

She also answered “No” on a March 2025 renewal application asking whether she was under investigation. That was months after FSRA sent her an inquiry letter.

The notice further alleged that typed notes she submitted as 2023 records had metadata showing they were created on Feb. 1.

What the case signals for Ontario mortgage brokers

The regulator’s April proposal against Trillium and three others also targeted the brokerage and its principal broker. It sought $60,000 from Trillium and $25,000 from principal broker Frank Manzo. It sought $80,000 and a compliance order against Khamar.

All four parties asked for hearings before the Financial Services Tribunal, and the allegations against the remaining three have not been proven. Kaur has undertaken to testify at a hearing on the merits. 

The case resembles FSRA’s decision to revoke Expert Financial Corporation’s brokerage licence over unlicensed activity. It also fits the trend in FSRA’s first enforcement annual report for 2024–25, which recorded 100 enforcement actions, up from 65 the previous year. 

“They’re finally taking seriously the role we play as mortgage professionals in the transaction. It’s frustrating to see the lack of professionalism [from some mortgage agents]. But I think what the latest regulation is doing is making the good ones even better and the bad ones are that much more obvious,” Joe Sammut, broker of record at Mortgage Architects, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this year.

FSRA said Khamar’s conduct left borrowers without the Act’s protections, including errors and omissions insurance. Joe White, founder and CEO of REMIC, made a similar point about licensing at MortgageFest Canada 2026, while discussing AI tools.

“Brokers are licensed. AI isn’t. The fact that brokers have errors and omissions insurance so that if something goes wrong, the client’s protected,” White said.

At the same event, Andy Kuyper, head of partnerships and secured lending at TransUnion, warned that the risk will grow as volumes recover.

“Fraud is a problem. It’s far easier for fraud to be committed when times are busy and everyone’s busy. So right now we’re in a good spot, but I would caution the industry to be careful as this industry rebounds – to be hypervigilant on fraud,” Kuyper said.

items.title: Suspended Markham brokerage kept dealing, Ontario regulator alleges
items.description: Alleged repeat disclosure failures could keep a Markham principal broker out of the business
items.content: <p>Alleged repeat disclosure failures could keep a Markham principal broker out of the business</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639277586609719389.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Alleged repeat disclosure failures could keep a Markham principal broker out of the business
items.body:
The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA) is moving to keep Renkai Lin out of the province’s mortgage brokering sector and to revoke the licence of his Markham brokerage, ZK Financial Inc.

The regulator alleges the pair kept arranging mortgages while suspended and gave it false information again, about a year after settling a similar case.

In a notice of proposal dated Sept. 2, Troy Harrison, FSRA’s acting director of litigation and enforcement, proposed refusing Lin’s April 9, application to reinstate his mortgage broker licence and revoking ZK Financial’s brokerage licence.

The notice said Lin, the brokerage’s principal broker and sole director, has shown “a pattern of unwillingness to comply with the requirements of the Act and regulations.”

The allegations have not been proven, and Lin and ZK Financial have requested a hearing before the Financial Services Tribunal.

A second round after a 2025 settlement

Lin held a licence from 2018 until May 8, 2025. ZK Financial was incorporated federally in October 2020 and licensed in January 2021.

In October 2024, FSRA moved against both for failing to disclose criminal charges laid in June 2022. The charges were missing from their 2023 and 2024 renewal applications and from their Annual Information Returns (AIRs), the yearly filings brokerages submit to the regulator.

Under an April 25, 2025, settlement, Lin and the brokerage admitted providing false or misleading information. They agreed to a $6,000 administrative penalty and a suspension.

A May 8, 2025, order required Lin to personally verify that every filing was accurate. On May 22, 2025, he was charged with further criminal offences, which remain before the courts.

FSRA now alleges Lin breached that condition. His reinstatement application left out a civil claim, issued Dec. 8, 2025, over brokerage fees on a mortgage renewal.

The regulator said he also left the lawsuit off the 2025 AIR, and that the 2024 and 2025 returns omitted mortgage and fee information he admitted in that proceeding.

Undisclosed proceedings have cost other licences. FSRA cited an inaccurate civil-proceedings declaration when it refused to renew the licence of broker Joel Kelman.

It also turned down a former principal broker who applied while criminal charges were outstanding, when it denied a broker licence to former Monarch Mortgage principal Victor Peca. 

What does the deposit rule mean for brokers?

FSRA says that between April 29 and June 1, ZK Financial took on a borrower while Lin was unlicensed and the brokerage was suspended. The notice identifies the borrower only as ZY and says the brokerage worked to arrange a mortgage of between $100,000 and $280,000.

According to the notice, Lin took a $2,000 deposit for his services and later refused to return it. Ontario Regulation 188/08 bars brokerages from requiring advance payments on mortgages of $400,000 or less.

FSRA also alleges that, during the suspension, ZK Financial’s website and 51.ca listings presented it as arranging a high volume of mortgages, which contradicted its 2025 AIR.

The regulator has drawn this line before. “Licensees must not facilitate activities for unlicensed individuals,” said Elissa Sinha, FSRA’s director of litigation and enforcement, when the regulator revoked the brokerage licence of Expert Financial Corporation. 

At MortgageFest Canada 2026, held in Toronto in September, Joe White, founder and chief executive of the Real Estate and Mortgage Institute of Canada (REMIC), argued that the licence itself is a broker’s core protection for clients. 

“Brokers are licensed. AI isn’t. The fact that brokers have errors and omissions insurance so that if something goes wrong, the client’s protected. AI can’t do that,” he said.

“What consumers will understand over time is that what they get with dealing with a broker is competency, and that takes years to create.”

Under Ontario Regulation 410/07, principal brokers must take reasonable steps to keep their brokerages compliant. FSRA alleges Lin failed to meet that duty.

The notice does not set a hearing date.

items.title: Expert: Canada’s Homes Got Cheaper In September, But Buyers Still Pulled Back
items.description:
Canadian homes got cheaper in September. Buyers responded by purchasing fewer of them. A falling price is welcome, but it does little for a household whose mortgage approval no longer covers the home.

There were 36,657 residential sales in September, 7.7% fewer than a year earlier. Sales fell 2.3% from August after seasonal adjustment, so the decline went beyond the usual seasonal change.

September residential sales, not seasonally adjusted; the annual comparison uses CREA’s revised figures. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

The national benchmark price fell 0.4% during September and was 3.4% below a year earlier. The average sale price fell 1.6% annually to $666,538. The benchmark tracks comparable housing attributes; the average also changes with the mix of homes sold.

Annual changes in the unadjusted national MLS® HPI and average sale price. The average is affected by the mix of transactions. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

A discount can disappear into the mortgage

CREA blames the weaker outlook on another increase in fixed mortgage rates and uncertainty over how far variable rates may rise. Its October forecast points to renewed energy-related inflation risks and a more hawkish Bank of Canada. The assumption of an easy return to cheaper borrowing has become harder to defend.

A buyer can negotiate thousands off the purchase price and still face a payment they cannot carry. How much of the discount survives depends on the mortgage size, rate and amortization. The asking price has come down; the lender has not necessarily become more generous.

There is more scope to negotiate than there was during the boom, but national listings are hardly overflowing. CREA counted slightly more than 200,000 homes for sale at the end of September, up just 1.8% annually and close to the historical norm.

B.C.’s supply problem looks different from Manitoba’s

Canada had 4.9 months of inventory after seasonal adjustment. British Columbia had 7.0 months, Manitoba 2.4, and Saskatchewan 3.4. Ontario was at 4.7. The ratio compares the stock of listings with the current sales pace.

Seasonally adjusted residential months of inventory by province. Local property types can differ substantially. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

Ontario’s sales-to-new-listings ratio was only 41.9%, even with fewer months of inventory than B.C. The first ratio compares purchases with new listings arriving that month. Months of inventory compares the stock already available with the current sales pace.

A buyer shopping for an apartment can face much less competition than someone looking for a detached home in the same city. Provincial totals are a poor substitute for checking the homes that actually fit the budget.

Ontario is doing worse than the national forecast

CREA forecasts a 0.2% increase in the national annual average sale price to $681,681 in 2026. Ontario’s average is forecast to fall 3% to $809,334, and B.C.’s to fall 0.8%. Gains elsewhere keep the national number slightly positive.

Ontario and B.C. are the two provinces with forecast annual average-price declines in 2026. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

Newfoundland and Labrador has the strongest expected average-price growth this year at 5.7%, followed by Saskatchewan at 5%. CREA expects both to slow in 2027, to 3.1% and 2.5% respectively.

The national average is projected to reach $689,909 in 2027, up 1.2%. Ontario’s forecast gain is 0.7%, to $815,100. These are nominal annual averages. Ontario’s projected increase next year would recover only a small part of this year’s forecast loss.

Annual average transaction prices in Canadian dollars. Forecast values are not December price targets. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

Five years later, parts of Ontario are still cheaper

Greater Toronto’s September benchmark was 14.7% below its September 2021 level. Hamilton-Burlington was down 15.3%. Calgary was 24.6% higher, Quebec City 54.4% higher and St. John’s 41.2% higher. These are seasonally adjusted composite benchmarks measured from September 2021, before the 2022 peak.

Five-year changes in seasonally adjusted composite MLS® HPI benchmarks, September 2021 to September 2026. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

For an owner in one of the weaker Ontario markets, waiting has already failed to guarantee a better sale price. Moving can mean accepting less equity than expected while financing the next purchase at a higher rate. That is a good reason for a household to stay put, even when it would rather move.

Developers also have to compete with the prices buyers can pay for existing homes. Softer resale prices can squeeze the revenue available to cover a new project’s costs. CREA’s releases do not track presales, construction costs, or developer balance sheets, so they cannot tell us which projects will proceed.

Pent-up demand still needs a mortgage

CREA now expects 444,530 sales in 2026 and 464,235 in 2027. The forecast rebound of 4.4% would leave annual sales 4,436 below 2025. Even the recovery scenario falls short of that earlier year’s activity.

The confident pitch about pent-up demand has become harder to hear over repeated forecast cuts. CREA still uses the term in its 2027 outlook, but buyers are expected to return after economic growth, renewed population growth and a clearer interest-rate path help them along. Calling demand pent-up does not make it financeable.

That forecast also assumes limited further action by the Bank of Canada. September showed how quickly higher borrowing costs can interrupt a recovery. Buyers may get a better price this fall, but they still have to live with the payment.


CREA’s September 2026 monthly statistics and MLS® HPI package and October 2026 housing forecast, released October 16, 2026. Statistics retain the comparisons and revisions in the supplied media PDFs. Annual forecast prices are nominal transaction averages; forecasts are scenarios, not observed outcomes.

Monthly statistics: https://stats.crea.ca/en-ca/

Quarterly forecasts (October media PDF; July comparison uses the official July 15 vintage): https://www.crea.ca/housing-market-stats/canadian-housing-market-stats/quarterly-forecasts/

Charts: valery.ca · Data: CREA. MLS® and Multiple Listing Service® are CREA trademarks. Independent analysis; no CREA affiliation or endorsement.

items.description: Rate-hike jitters are pushing buyers to the sidelines as the Canadian housing market braces for a slower end to the year
items.content: <p>Rate-hike jitters are pushing buyers to the sidelines as the Canadian housing market braces for a slower end to the year</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639277543854804701.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Rate-hike jitters are pushing buyers to the sidelines as the Canadian housing market braces for a slower end to the year
items.body:
The Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) has lowered its home sales forecast for a third straight quarter, now projecting 444,530 residential transactions through Multiple Listing Service® (MLS®) Systems.

That would be a 5.2% drop from 2025, as rising fixed mortgage rates and the threat of a Bank of Canada hike sideline buyers.

The October 16 revision strips 18,806 sales from CREA’s July estimate, when the association expected a far milder 1.4% annual decline in home sales.

The national average price is now forecast to edge up just 0.2% to $681,681, roughly $5,000 below the summer call.

How rising fixed mortgage rates hit September home sales

CREA said oil prices began climbing again in early September while the Bank of Canada struck a more hawkish tone, with markets now pricing in approximately 100 basis points of hikes by this time next year.

The five-year Government of Canada bond yield, which lenders use to price fixed mortgages, closed at 3.60% on October 2, up from 3.35% on September 1.

September sales fell 2.3% from August and 7.7% from a year earlier. The national average sale price was $666,538, down 1.6% year over year.

Lenders saw the repricing coming.

“I think rates will probably go up in October. GIC rates are up 35 points in the last sixty to ninety days. Bank of Canada bond rates are up 60 points. Like everything’s been going up already. So it’s just a natural part of the market,” Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthOne Bank of Canada, said at MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September.

Victor Tran, a mortgage agent at Tango Financial in Toronto, is already seeing borrowers rethink their options.

“The variable-rate forecast isn’t looking too good either,” Tran told Canadian Mortgage Professional as bond markets turned volatile in September.

“So we have people sitting in variable rates considering locking into fixed rates, for example.”

Tracy Valko, founder of AIMI Mortgage Collective, said brokers need to be able to explain those forces to clients.

“There’s a lot of global tensions right now that are affecting our market. What’s affecting bond yields? What affects fixed rates? Agents and brokers should know that. We as mortgage agents and brokers should never predict, but one thing we should do is make sure that we understand the knowledge so we can future-prepare homeowners for what could be coming down the pipeline,” Valko said at the event.

Ontario and BC weigh on 2026 home prices

CREA expects Ontario’s average price to fall 3% to $809,334 and British Columbia’s to slip 0.8% to $944,685 this year, while Newfoundland and Labrador (5.7%) and Saskatchewan (5%) lead gains.

For 2027, it forecasts a 4.4% rebound to 464,235 sales and a 1.2% price gain to $689,909, assuming limited action from the central bank. Even that recovery would leave sales about 4,400 below 2025 levels.

Andy Kuyper, head of partnerships and secured lending at TransUnion, was cautious on timing.

“I’d like to be optimistic. I think we’re facing the reality that with the geopolitical climate and everything that’s happening here, our mortgage industry is probably not ready to rebound. We are seeing slight growth in originations, we’re seeing slight growth in mortgage balances – a lot more on the refi side,” he said at MortgageFest.

Brokers say the slowdown raises the value of advice over price.

“Now more than ever it’s so important for people to use a mortgage broker rather than their bank, because the banks are specifically just focusing on rates. As we head into a turbulent time where potentially we will see an increase in rates, the banks are putting clients in, say, a variable rate, which may not be the best option for that client – just because it has a three in front of it,” said Sabeena Bubber, a mortgage broker at Xeva Mortgage.

Valko expects little relief. “The next two years are going to be very similar to what we’re dealing with right now. Staying a best-rate mortgage broker is not going to get you the goals that you want,” she said.

Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres (DLC), expects a hike by late 2026 or the first half of 2027.

“We have to expect higher interest rates, which also means that fixed-rate mortgages are very attractive now,” she said.

The Bank of Canada’s next rate decision is October 28.

items.title: How credit unions are navigating a turbulent 2026 market
items.description: CEO spells out careful approach in a lending environment marked by risk and plenty of volatility
items.content: <p>CEO spells out careful approach in a lending environment marked by risk and plenty of volatility</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639276728476168839.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: CEO spells out careful approach in a lending environment marked by risk and plenty of volatility
items.body:
Canada’s current housing market is moribund, according to a leading community lending chief executive officer. And that means credit unions are navigating a difficult balancing act: maintaining volumes without taking on undue risk in a market where prices are still falling.

Fausto Gaudio, president and chief executive officer of the Toronto-headquartered IC Savings, described the current market as one where activity was barely getting off the ground. “It’s very, very soft,” he told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “Softer than it was last year – and last year was also a very soft year in terms of trades and prices declining as well.”

That marks one of the biggest obstacles facing credit unions and other lenders. Maintaining asset size is no easy feat, but loosening credit standards to bring more business in isn’t always the best idea either as values continue to slide.

“Top of mind is that there just isn’t enough volume,” Gaudio said. “It’s very, very difficult… to maintain asset size, because unless we expand our risk tolerance and do mortgages at a higher loan-to-value at a time when prices are declining. That’s a real challenge, especially for small boutique lenders.”

Gaudio said IC Savings has opted to hold its position rather than chase volume, steering clear of high-LTV lending. “We do very few mortgages at the 80% loan-to-value,” he said. “And so we don’t seem to have a lot of the problems that the big banks have in terms of defaults and powers of sale today.”

But there’s also opportunity in the market, not least in serving borrowers who fall outside standard bank approval criteria. Tighter lending standards among Canada’s banking giants mean borrowers often don’t qualify in the current market not because of recklessness, but rather circumstance.

When dealing with those customers, understanding the story – and the “why” of how their current situation developed – is crucial, according to Gaudio.

“With somebody that might have had a difficulty – having gone through a health problem, a period of unemployment, a marital breakup – we’re much more attentive to those human stories and try to resolve their problems,” he said.

“When a borrower is coming out of a life experience and a setback, we’re much more willing to try to resolve their issue – but at the same time, they need to have some equity to offset that risk.”

Reverse mortgages: Will their popularity grow in the credit union space?

Gaudio said IC Savings has developed a new term reverse mortgage, a fixed-period alternative to the traditional lifetime arrangement, aimed at homeowners who want to access equity but have a clear exit plan within a few years.

The product, he said, is for “someone that wants to live in their house another three or possibly five years, but then they have a plan – to move back to Northern Ontario or the East Coast where they had family or grandkids – but they don’t want to commit to a reverse mortgage for life.”

2027 outlook for wider market remains unclear

Gaudio sees the current housing market sluggishness as a product of rampant unaffordability rather than the geopolitical headwinds hovering over the Canadian economy.

Trade turmoil and rising oil prices, he said, have less impact of the housing market than the fact that prices have skyrocketed over the past decade, and remain elevated in many regions despite the years-long cooldown.

It remains unclear whether the broader market will normalize quickly enough to ease volume pressure on boutique lenders heading into 2027, but with borrower stress likely to continue rising, he emphasized the importance of brokers and agents telling their customer’s story in as much detail as possible to boost their chances of getting a deal through.

“I believe the brokers that deal with us know us as that type of lender,” he said.

items.title: ‘No to the nine’ vs. ‘yes to the rest’: The impact of Alberta’s other nine referendum questions
items.description: Both in Alberta and nationwide, the focus of Monday’s referendum has been on the question of separation. But that’s just one of 10 questions being put to Albertans.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Voters leave a polling station after casting ballots in an Alberta byelection for the Olds-Didsbury-Three Hills riding, in Cremona, Alta., Monday, June 23, 2025.THE CANADIAN PRESS/Jeff McIntosh]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Jeff McIntosh</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Both in Alberta and nationwide, the focus of Monday’s referendum has been on the question of separation. But that’s just one of 10 questions being put to Albertans.
items.body:
CTV News is your Alberta Referendum headquarters. Live results. Expert analysis. Everything you need to know is here.

Both in Alberta and nationwide, the focus of Monday’s referendum has been on the question of separation. But that’s just one of 10 questions being put to Albertans.

In a variety of camps, the others are referred to as “the nine.”

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Alberta’s Voice, a grassroot remain campaign, has a “no to the nine” lawn sign, while some separatists, frustrated with Premier Danielle Smith, are promoting their own boycott with the phrase “decline the 9.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney weighed in on the topic for the first time Thursday and encouraged a Calgary crowd to make sure they mark their ballots, “including, ‘No to the Nine.’”

Smith responded a social media post repeating her counter message of “yes to the rest.”

The nine questions themselves can be split into two groups:

Four ask whether the province should work to change Canada’s Constitution, on topics ranging from abolishing the Senate to allowing provinces to opt out of federal programs, such as health care, without losing federal funding.

The other five are connected to immigration, including whether the province should have more control over the system in Alberta, and whether it should charge a fee to those with a “non-permanent immigration status” for health care and education.

What impact would the nine have nationwide?

Experts say no matter the outcome of Monday’s vote, nothing tangible will change the next day for either Alberta or the rest of Canada.

“It’s almost irrelevant because they’re not binding,” Concordia University economics professor Moshe Lander told CTV News from Calgary. “They don’t actually mean anything in terms of Confederation, in terms of the Constitution, in terms of law.”

Any changes to the Constitution are complicated, with many on Alberta’s list requiring support of seven provinces that represent at least 50 per cent of Canada’s population. Abolishing the Senate would require consent of all 10 provinces, the House of Commons and the Senate itself.

While no tangible change is expected next week in any referendum outcome, whether a message from a potential “yes” vote to the other nine could resonate with Canadians elsewhere is a different question.

“If Alberta says that we can openly be a little more aggressive, not just being anti-immigrant, but even trying to cut them off from public services, yes, it could encourage other provinces to say, ‘Well, if they get a chance to say that, why don’t we get a chance to say that?’” Lander said.

He also said Alberta has traditionally been viewed as “kind of a wild west.”

“Even if Albertans say, ‘Yeah, we’re not too fond of immigrants,’ or, ‘Yeah, we want to try and wrestle control over policies that have traditionally been federal-level decisions,’ there is the possibility that the rest of Canada just shrugs and says, ‘Well, there’s Alberta being Alberta again.’”

Mount Royal University political science professor Duane Bratt believes a “yes” on immigration questions could influence other provinces to make similar moves.

“Because we have seen a breakdown in the immigration consensus over the last few years, something that even the Trudeau government and the Carney government have recognized,” the political analyst told CTV News.

On questions involving constitutional change, Bratt said it will be easy to find some “synergies” between Alberta and Quebec, such as on federal spending power, and the power to name judges. But he added it will be “much tougher” to get buy in from other provinces and the federal government.

“So, I want to see what transpires, and this could be a problem for (Smith) after the referendum, if she is seen to be working closely with a separatist government in Quebec,” Bratt said.

Lander said a “yes” to constitutional questions could encourage any provinces that may have been quietly considering similar questions to push for broader constitutional discussions, something that hasn’t happened since the Meech Lake Accord in 1987.

“Personally, I don’t think that the Alberta questions are meaningful in any way, but I do agree that hey, this is a full generation past,” Lander said. “In order to keep that Constitution fresh and relevant, it’s not that it has to be changed. It’s just that it has to be reread and maybe reviewed. And I don’t think that there’s necessarily anything wrong with that.”

Political analyst Lori Williams “it’s certainly possible” other provinces would want to see changes in the wake of Alberta, but pointed to the difficult reality of changing the Constitution.

“We’ve seen when we start talking about constitutional amendments, different provinces want different things, and getting an agreement on a unanimous, or even a seven out of 10 provinces, agreement on some of these questions has proved very difficult in Canadian history,” Williams said.

Do we know how people will vote?

There is far less polling available on the expected outcomes of the nine as there is on the separation question, but one from last summer found 60 per cent support for the immigration-related questions, and around 40 per cent for the constitutional topics. That was before some in the separatist movement encouraged boycotting the nine.

And according to Williams, most Albertans only started paying closer attention to the nine questions in the last few weeks. She described the polling process on them as “quite difficult.”

“As pollsters actually read the questions, people get confused or impatient, and so we don’t have a really good set of numbers on the individual questions. There have been some polls that have indicated varying levels of support,” she told CTV News.

Williams has spoken to thousands of Albertans on both sides of the debate as she has led information sessions put on by community groups over the past few months. She has seen a lot of confusion around the nine questions and thinks that will impact the response rate.

“People who don’t quite understand what the questions mean are wondering whether they absolutely have to answer those … a lot of people that are frustrated and overwhelmed,” she said.

Bratt believes there’s “a good chance” none of the nine will pass, or if they do, it will be narrowly.

“‘No to the Nine,’ it has been gaining traction, and the separatist movement, who would endorse … these other nine questions are being told to boycott them, because they all involve staying in Canada,” Bratt said. “And if the separatists don’t vote on them, I don’t know how they pass.”

Williams said it will be important to watch whether fewer people vote on the other nine than the separation question, and how that may influence a provincial mandate.

“Is a 50 per cent plus-one vote that was cast by only 30 per cent of those who voted in the campaign, is that enough to give the province a mandate or not? I think questions like that will emerge,” she said.

Whatever happens Monday, due to the complicated nature of having to hand count 10 separate ballots that involve marking 10 pieces of paper put into 10 envelopes and then 10 separate ballot boxes, no one expects to learn an immediate outcome. Separation question responses will be counted first.

Bratt predicts there may not be an answer on the other nine until Wednesday or Thursday. Williams agrees it “could be late in the week.”

items.title: What persistently high bond yields could mean for the commercial mortgage market
items.description: Avison Young flags cap rate pressure as lenders tighten underwriting on income properties
items.content: <p>Avison Young flags cap rate pressure as lenders tighten underwriting on income properties</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639276802996438662.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Avison Young flags cap rate pressure as lenders tighten underwriting on income properties
items.body:
Persistently high long-term bond yields are shaping up as the deciding variable for Canada’s commercial mortgage market, with Avison Young warning that capitalization rates may struggle to hold if borrowing costs stay elevated into 2027.

In its Q3 2026 Canadian cap rate and investment trends report, the real estate services firm said yields no longer move on central bank policy alone, with persistent inflation, government borrowing, trade disruptions, energy markets and geopolitical tension lifting financing costs and investors’ required returns.

The cap rate, a property’s net operating income divided by its value, is where that pressure lands. Higher cap rates mean lower valuations and smaller loans for income-property clients.

National benchmarks sat at 4.55% for high-density urban multifamily, 5.85% for new single-tenant industrial and 6.90% for downtown class A office in the third quarter, following a second quarter in which Toronto anchored Canada’s commercial real estate rebound.

The five-year Government of Canada bond yield closed at 3.60% on October 2, up from 3.35% on September 1, according to Bank of Canada data, extending an oil-fuelled bond selloff that pushed Canada’s 10-year yield to 3.9% in September. 

“Bond markets are essentially doing some of the Bank of Canada’s job for them,” RBC economist Carrie Freestone said on the bank’s The 10-Minute Take podcast, as bond yields are already repricing Canada’s fixed mortgage market.

How are lenders pricing commercial mortgage risk?

Credit is still flowing, but on tighter terms. Conventional multifamily loans price 130 to 200 basis points over the five-year Government of Canada yield.

Loans insured by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) price 55 to 100 basis points over it, the survey said.

Office spreads run 150 to 250 basis points. Multifamily arrears are trending up, and CMHC-insured applications fell from the prior quarter.

“While capital remains available across all asset classes, uncertainty related to geopolitical tensions, trade disruption, and rising bond yields is beginning to reduce borrowing capacity and increase lender caution,” said Ron Dezman, senior vice-president, debt capital and advisory, at Avison Young in Edmonton.

"In the CMHC lending market, underwriting assumptions for rental growth and threshold interest rates are becoming more conservative as supply risk deepens across several markets."

What higher yields mean for brokers’ commercial clients

Private investors made 48% of third-quarter acquisitions worth $5 million or more, according to CoStar data in the report. Mortgage renewal or maturity ranked as the second-most common reason owners sold multifamily assets.

“For multifamily pricing, bond yields will be the dominant story for the remainder of 2026, as a persistence of higher yields will likely place upward pressure on cap rates, especially with the relatively flat near-term income growth expectations,” said Carey Buntain, principal, capital markets, at Avison Young in Vancouver.

Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthOne Bank of Canada, flagged the move at MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September.

“I think rates will probably go up in October. GIC rates are up 35 points in the last sixty to ninety days. Bank of Canada bond rates are up 60 points. Like everything’s been going up already. So it’s just a natural part of the market,” Armstrong said.

items._ogDesc: Canadian bond yields are rising as hot US inflation is driving market expectations of four rate hikes from the Bank of Canada.
items.body:
The cross-border flow of goods is slow, but Canada’s imports of American inflation are ramping up. Government of Canada (GoC) short-term bond yields have climbed sharply since February. Gas prices were behind the initial surge, but yields are still climbing after gas stalled. A new report from BMO Capital Markets attributes the continued rise to hot U.S. inflation. The bank warns that markets are pricing in a full point of rate hikes from the Bank of Canada (BoC) by the end of 2027.

Canadian Bond Yields Pushed Higher By Hot U.S. Inflation

Higher gas prices have driven Canadian bond yields (and inflation) higher since February. BoC Governor Tiff Macklem warned yesterday that “every major central bank is worried…” because “…these costs have to go somewhere,” highlights BMO chief economist Douglas Porter.

Porter’s research shows the GoC 2-year bond yield’s correlation with gas prices at r=0.8, 1.0 being a perfect correlation. Gas prices and bond yields are moving very closely together, with the divergence only starting in September. Gas prices stabilized that month, but Canadian short- and medium-term yields rose further.

Porter flags the strong US jobs report as the catalyst that month. It was followed by a US Federal Reserve speech at Jackson Hole that was hawkish, suggesting the economy is running too hot. American inflation reported yesterday reinforced those concerns, as annual growth hit 3.7% in September, well above the 2% target.

Canadian yields are responding to that pressure, in addition to the energy bump. “Accordingly, the warm U.S. CPI has bumped Canadian yields again, with 2s backing up to 3.25%,” warns Porter.

Markets Expect Canadian Rates Will Rise 1 Point

Canada’s 2-year government bond yield hit 3.25% this week, reflecting expectations of tighter monetary policy. “That’s a full 100 bps above overnight rates, and the market is indeed expecting that much tightening by end-2027,” explains Porter.

The aggressive rise means higher mortgage rates may be ahead. A full point added to the overnight rate would trickle directly into variable rates. Fixed-rate mortgages are driven by bond yields, meaning they’re likely to lead here. BMO questions whether that much tightening is warranted while tariffs and trade uncertainty weigh on Canada. “That seems like a lot,” bluntly states Porter.

BMO Questions Scale of Tightening Amid Weak Economy

The market may be pricing in higher rates, but Canada’s economy may not be able to handle them. “Now, GoC yields are being largely pulled by domestic data—the weak jobs data helped pull them lower—and U.S. yields,” explains Porter.

Porter isn’t dismissing rate hikes, but suggests that market expectations are inflated. Higher rates would throttle demand, reducing inflation further. However, there’s still the matter of currency value that Porter doesn’t address. The situation the BoC faces is a little more complicated than just a demand issue.

Global commodities such as oil, wheat, and corn are generally priced in US dollars. That’s even the case for Canadian oil, which is priced based on global demand. Weak consumption can cool domestic price pressure, but a weaker loonie can still raise import costs. If hot US inflation keeps American rates elevated while Canadian weakness calls for relief, the BoC faces a difficult trade-off. A policy miss could deepen the slowdown or prolong inflation, raising stagflation risks.

items.title: Customer satisfaction with top banks grows – but there’s a catch
items.description: Younger Canadians are eyeing fintechs as fees and rates loosen their loyalty to traditional banks
items.content: <p>Younger Canadians are eyeing fintechs as fees and rates loosen their loyalty to traditional banks</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0321_638766022774937297.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Younger Canadians are eyeing fintechs as fees and rates loosen their loyalty to traditional banks
items.body:
Canadians are slightly happier with their banks this year, but the gain hides a loyalty problem that could reshape where younger borrowers take their business.

Overall customer satisfaction rose 3 points on a 1,000-point scale, lifted mainly by the Big 5 banks, according to the JD Power 2026 Canada Retail Banking Satisfaction Study.

However, fintechs – newer online banks – outscored both the Big 5 and midsize banks on many factors that drive satisfaction, and they are drawing a disproportionate share of younger Canadians planning to move their primary banking relationship.

Among Gen Z and Gen Y customers of traditional retail banks, 17% said they probably or definitely will switch primary banks within 12 months, a five-year high.

Four of the five leading reasons involve product offerings such as fees, interest rates and promotions.

“Younger customers can be satisfied with their bank and still leave if they see a better opportunity to save money elsewhere,” said Paul McAdam, senior director of banking and payments intelligence at JD Power.

“When household budgets are tight, a monthly banking fee becomes an expense worth reconsidering.”

RBC ranked highest among the Big 5 for a third straight year at 619. BMO and CIBC tied for second at 611, with TD close behind in fourth at 610.

Among midsize banks, Tangerine Bank took the top spot for a 15th consecutive year at 676, followed by ATB Financial at 650.

Why are younger bank customers ready to leave?

The findings echo an Equifax Canada survey showing most mortgage holders would consider switching lenders at renewal. Tracy Valko, founder of AIMI Mortgage Collective, described the financial strain behind that restlessness at MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September.

“One out of two Canadians are $200 away from not meeting their financial obligations every month. And that’s profound. We never had this before. And they need that empathy – to see as a mortgage broker that you care about that,” she said.

The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) says frontier AI is among the fastest-growing threats facing lenders, warning that advanced models can help adversaries identify and exploit vulnerabilities at greater speed and scale. https://t.co/B9plArK6ju — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 12, 2026

What the bank switching trend means for mortgage brokers

A client willing to leave a bank over a monthly fee is a client willing to shop at renewal. Valko, who joined MortgageFest Canada’s Day 1 panel on the path forward for brokers, said winning that client takes more than price.

“As an industry, we got away from where it was about transactions and how many deals you did. Now it’s about focusing on that financial plan and strategy for that client, building that long-term financial relationship. So you look like a true expert and not just a rate agent.”

Prakash Bector, vice-president of national sales and distribution at EQ Bank, sees the opening.

"It's just staying focused on what we have in our control. So from a broker standpoint, it's those consistent outreaches to clients, leveraging your database, building new referral sources," she said during the mortgage event.

“As challenging as the market is, there’s immense opportunity for brokers. I think brokers’ share will continue to grow. A lot of clients need sound advice right now – they’re struggling, they don’t know what’s going to happen next. And this is where brokers play a critical role.”

Technology is part of that pitch, though not as advice. Fraud prevention and data security topped customers’ preferred uses of bank AI at 31%, against 12% for personal financial advice, a useful signal for brokers weighing how mortgage professionals can keep up with AI.

JD Power surveyed 14,038 retail banking customers in two waves during 2026.

items.title: Royal LePage: trade tensions stall Canada’s fall housing market
items.description: Rate hike fears and tariffs keep buyers waiting as brokers head into a slower autumn
items.content: <p>Rate hike fears and tariffs keep buyers waiting as brokers head into a slower autumn</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/073/0388_639276754438511603.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Rate hike fears and tariffs keep buyers waiting as brokers head into a slower autumn
items.body:
Canada’s housing market stalled in the third quarter of 2026 as new US tariffs and the prospect of higher mortgage rates kept buyers sidelined, according to the Royal LePage House Price Survey and Market Forecast.

The national aggregate home price slipped 0.8% year over year to $810,000 and fell 0.6% from the second quarter. Royal LePage now forecasts a 1.0% annual gain in the fourth quarter, down from the 2.0% it projected in its second-quarter house price survey.

Greater Toronto Area prices fell 3.7% to $1,073,100, while Greater Vancouver dropped 4.0% to $1,148,100.

Greater Montreal bucked the trend with a 2.9% gain to $653,700, and Prairie markets held steadier.

The trade dispute escalated after talks collapsed on Aug. 21 and Washington imposed a 50% tariff on a wide range of Canadian goods a day later.

“For many buyers, the hesitation is less about what they can afford today than how secure they feel about tomorrow,” said Phil Soper, president and CEO of Royal LePage.

“Buyers have more negotiating power, but little control over the forces shaping their confidence.”

BMO senior economist Sal Guatieri flagged the same risk in April.

“Unfortunately, it’s the economic uncertainty – both related to the trade war and the Iran war – that will likely keep a lot of buyers, especially first-time buyers, on the sidelines,” he said.

Royal LePage home prices by market, Q3 2026

Aggregate and median prices, with Royal LePage’s year-end forecast

*Forecast change in aggregate price, Q4 2026 vs. Q4 2025. Prices include resale and new build. Negative figures shown in red.
Source: Royal LePage House Price Survey and Market Forecast, Q3 2026 (released Oct. 15, 2026); price data from RPS Real Property Solutions

Mortgage rate jitters fail to pull buyers forward

The Bank of Canada has held its overnight rate at 2.25% for a year, with announcements due Oct. 28 and Dec. 9. Soper expects a hold through 2026 and a hike in early 2027, though a growing number of forecasters are calling for an October rate hike.

Yet the threat of costlier borrowing has not created urgency. “Low confidence is outweighing the urgency to lock in today’s favourable borrowing costs,” Soper said.

Renewals add another layer of pressure. The Royal LePage 2026 Mortgage Renewal Survey found 38% of mortgage holders expect higher payments at renewal.

Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthOne Bank of Canada, is among those expecting an earlier move.

“I think rates will probably go up in October. GIC rates are up 35 points in the last sixty to ninety days. Bank of Canada bond rates are up 60 points. Like everything’s been going up already. So it’s just a natural part of the market,” he shared during MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September.

Yet the threat of costlier borrowing has not created urgency. “Low confidence is outweighing the urgency to lock in today’s favourable borrowing costs,” Soper said.

Renewals add another layer of pressure. The Royal LePage 2026 Mortgage Renewal Survey found 38% of mortgage holders expect higher payments at renewal. Armstrong argued the risk is manageable.

“I think everyone got really worried about the renewal cliff. So they got really good at preparing for it. And I think that preparation has taken the noise out of it,” he said.

“We’re in normal rates today. We’re not in obscenely high rates. So I think the renewal cliff doesn’t exist to the extreme, but it’s something we need to be aware of.”

Don Kottick of RE/MAX Canada says buyers remain willing to make compromises, from relocating farther from city centres to adjusting their spending habits, to achieve their homeownership goals. https://t.co/GOHrsHlsWY — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 14, 2026

What brokers are seeing on the ground

For buyers who do act, leverage has shifted. “Conditions of finance are back in. Home inspections, everything, you name it. Water testing. We have price reductions,” said Sarita Free, a mortgage agent with Mortgage Powered Financial Group in Norfolk County, Ont., who spoke at MortgageFest.

Tracy Valko, founder of AIMI Mortgage Collective, said brokers must understand the macro picture without guessing at it.

“There’s a lot of global tensions right now that are affecting our market. What’s affecting bond yields? What affects fixed rates? Agents and brokers should know that. We as mortgage agents and brokers should never predict, but one thing we should do is make sure that we understand the knowledge so we can future-prepare homeowners for what could be coming down the pipeline,” she explained during the mortgage event.

Andy Kuyper, head of partnerships and secured lending at TransUnion, sees a slow climb rather than a rebound and also shared his thoughts during MortgageFest Canada.

“I’d like to be optimistic. I think we’re facing the reality that with the geopolitical climate and everything that’s happening here, our mortgage industry is probably not ready to rebound. We are seeing slight growth in originations, we’re seeing slight growth in mortgage balances – a lot more on the refi side,” he said.

Soper remains measured. “Canada’s housing market is on a detour, not a derailment,” he said.

items.title: Terra Bona’s Two-Tower Development Site In Markham Sold Under Receivership
items.description:
After being placed under receivership last December, the Grandview Tower project in Markham, Ontario has officially been sold, according to filings in Ontario Superior Court.

The project was set for 7115 Yonge Street plus 8, 10, 12, and 14 Grandview Avenue; a 0.95-acre site on the eastern side of Yonge Street between Meadowview Avenue and Grandview Avenue, about three blocks north of Centerpoint Mall.

The site consists of a vacant parcel of land and four single-family lots that Terra Bona Developments Ltd. was planning to redevelop. The original proposal was for a 36-storey condo tower with 443 units before it was later revised — following an appeal to the Ontario Land Tribunal — to one 49-storey tower and one 46-storey tower, with a grand total of 873 residential units.

For the project, Terra Bona — through Terrabona 7115 Yonge Ltd. — secured a first-ranking mortgage from Toronto-based Empirical Capital Corp. in October 2022 for the principal amount of $31,000,000, with interest accruing at the greater of 10.25% per annum or the RBC Prime Rate + 4.80%.

The loan was guaranteed by Majid Tavakoli and Majid Tavakoli Holdings Ltd.

According to loan documents filed in the proceeding, the purpose of the loan was to repay existing mortgages, fund a partner buy-out, and pay various fees. The existing mortgages that were taken out with the loan consisted of $15,777,261 owed to Forgestone Capital, and $4,311,000 owed to MarshallZehr.

The Receivership

According to court documents, Empirical Capital first initiated the receivership proceedings in November 2024 after Terra Bona defaulted on the loan when they failed to make an interest payment in May 2024.

Terra Bona then provided a proposal that would see them take out a second mortgage and make a significant paydown to Empirical in exchange for extending the maturity date of the loan from July 2024 to August 2025.

However, Empirical says Terra Bona was unable to secure that financing, and Empirical made a formal demand for payment in September 2024. The borrower was still unable to pay, and Empirical subsequently initiated the receivership proceeding, saying they were owed $33,419,371,06 as of January 1, 2025, with interest continuing to accrue.

The original proposal (left) and current proposal (right) for 7115 Yonge Street and 8-14 Grandview Avenue in Markam. (Arcadis)

“I verily believe the Debtor is insolvent and unable to fulfil its obligations to the Lender and the other creditors,” said Empirical in an affidavit. “It does not appear to have the financial capability to proceed with the since May of 2024 and the Debtor appears to be unable to make any payment on account of the Loan.”

Before the receivership application was granted, however, the two sides entered into a forbearance agreement delaying enforcement until June 2025. According to the forbearance agreement, the developer was in discussions with Metrolinx at the time about three temporary easements, and was also awaiting a 13-day OLT hearing in May 2025.

However, Terra Bona defaulted on the forbearance agreement, they were still unable to repay the loan, and the receivership application was recommenced and granted on December 1, 2025.

The Sale

In late-January 2026, the court-appointed Receiver then retained Lennard Commercial Realty to list the property, with Peter DeGuerre, Joshua Perlstein, and Paul Campbell serving as the listing team, beating out proposals by Cushman & Wakefield, CBRE, and Colliers.

“This offering represents a rare opportunity to acquire a high-density, transit-oriented development site with a Yonge Street address,” said Lennard Commercial Realty in its sales brochure. “With full approvals secured through the Ontario Land Tribunal (OLT) Order (Case No. OLT-24-000601) issued Nov 12, 2025, the site offers a rare opportunity to develop a landmark high-rise development in this highly accessible and sought-after North York corridor.”

According to a report prepared by the Receiver dated September 11, 2026, Lennard marketed the property, 28 interested parties reached the point of signing a confidentiality agreement, and a total of seven offers were received.

In June, the Receiver entered into a sale agreement with 2158046 Ontario Inc., which waived its conditions on August 19. The true purchaser was not identified, but a copy of the sales agreement included in court filings was signed by Shane Baghai, a luxury condo developer operated by the company’s namesake.

The purchase price was not disclosed, but the Receiver said Empirical was owed $39,167,304.23 as of August 24, 2026 and said “It is anticipated that Empirical will suffer a shortfall,” suggesting the purchase price was lower than the outstanding debt.

Comparable transactions Lennard cited in a report included the sales of 7-17 Nipigon Avenue for $26,623,000, the sale of 26-34 Nipigon Avenue for $19,350,000, and the sale of 41-47 Hendon Way for $15,350,000, all of which occurred in 2024 and 2025.

items.title: Housing coalition outlines four demands ahead of B.C. election
items.description: Developers and affordable housing providers urge parties to restore planned investments and reduce development costs
items._ogDesc: Developers and affordable housing providers urge parties to restore planned investments and reduce development costs
items.body:
Market-rate developers and non-profit housing providers are joining forces to urge B.C.’s political parties to reduce the cost of building homes, warning that rising expenses and policy uncertainty are leaving projects stalled.

The Urban Development Institute (UDI), B.C. Non-Profit Housing Association (BCNPHA), Aboriginal Housing Management Association (AHMA) and Co-operative Housing Federation of B.C. (CHF BC) on Tuesday called on all parties to commit to four measures aimed at making housing development more financially viable.

The groups said the cost of building and financing homes in B.C. has exceeded what many buyers can afford and what governments are willing to subsidize for low- and moderate-income renters, resulting in projects failing to get off the drawing board.

“When market developers and non-profit housing providers are asking for the same thing, it should tell every party how serious the cost of delivery crisis is,” said Mike Drummond, CEO of UDI, in a statement.

The groups are asking the next provincial government to restore planned investments in non-profit, co-operative and Indigenous housing, allowing more than 5,000 affordable rental homes that were deferred following $1.4 billion in recent budget cuts to proceed.

“The projects are ready, but the land sits empty,” said Jill Atkey, CEO of the B.C. Non-Profit Housing Association.

“The people waiting for affordable housing cannot wait another budget cycle. The next government has an opportunity to restore the investment and get these homes built.”

The coalition also called on the government to co-invest remaining BC Rental Protection Funds with the Canada Rental Protection Fund to “continue protecting the affordability that already exists in the market.”

In addition, the groups urged the next government to finalize a federal-provincial agreement to reduce development cost charges and fund infrastructure needed to support new housing within 90 days of forming government.

The federal and provincial governments announced a 10-year partnership in June under which they would each contribute nearly $1.6 billion to reduce development charges for multi-unit housing by up to 50 per cent in priority communities and fund infrastructure.

“The details were not finalized before the election was called, so builders cannot price it into projects and municipalities cannot act on it,” said the coalition in a statement Tuesday.

Lastly, the groups called for a federal GST exemption on new homes for all eligible buyers rather than limiting relief to first-time purchasers. They pointed to Ontario’s expanded HST rebate program, announced in March, which temporarily eliminated the 13 per cent HST on eligible buyers of new homes valued at $1 million or less.

“The commitments made in 2024 need to translate into homes on the ground,” said Margaret Pfoh, CEO of the Aboriginal Housing Management Association, in a statement.
